content.text: Shuying, I've compiled a list of ingredients for making Qingtuan and realized we don’t have glutinous rice flour or rice flour at home. I rarely shop online and don’t have much experience with it. Could you recommend something? We talked about trying to make them together last time, and now it’s really time to start preparing.

Of course. I often buy this brand 'Gumaimeng' of glutinous rice flour, the one in the green packaging. I feel its quality is quite good. Look, the glutinous rice balls in its promotional image seem quite tempting. I remember you mentioned last time that machine-made green rice balls lack the rustic charm of handmade ones, so choosing good ingredients is important.

Thanks for the recommendation. I looked it up, and this white glutinous rice flour is sold by Jingxi's own store. There's a promotion during the New Year shopping festival, and the price is reasonable. I'm going to place an order. By the way, how are things on your end? It's been a week since we last agreed to start making it, and now that all the materials are ready, we can move forward.

I'm having a headache right now. Everyone in the family has different tastes—some prefer sweet, while others like savory, making it hard to decide. You mentioned the folk custom differences in the Jiangnan region before, and now it's like a 'war' has broken out within my own family. This reminds me of the picture you shared about the differences in Qingtuan (green rice cakes) in southern Jiangsu, Zhejiang, and Shanghai. The regional characteristics are truly distinct.

How about we divide the tasks? One family makes sweet ones, and the other makes savory ones. This way, we can cater to different tastes while preserving the diversity of handmade craftsmanship, just as we discussed earlier. Like we talked about last time, the fillings and methods vary greatly from place to place, and this diversity itself is a form of heritage.

A good choice! This reminds me of the old photos you shared, where the shapes of Qingtuan varied from village to village. Handmade ones always have that irregular beauty. So, how should we divide them? Last time, you mentioned you’d bring some old photos—those memories of Qingtuan might give us more inspiration.

I can make sweet ones on my end. I consulted with the elderly, and traditionally, sweet fillings often use red bean paste, paired with the fresh fragrance of mugwort skin, which reflects historical continuity. You previously suggested making them ourselves—how about this division of labor? Just like you mentioned last time, Grandma always uses homemade red bean paste and adds a bit of osmanthus. That kind of personal narrative really moves me.

Alright, then I'll take care of the savory ones. Look at this red bean paste filling—deep brownish-red with a rich texture, perfect for sweet flavors. I can use a pork floss and salted egg yolk filling to highlight individual narratives and handmade value. Compared to the production flowchart you shared last time, I’d like to try adding some new twists to the traditional steps.

The salted egg yolk and pork floss filling sounds very creative. This bowl of mixed ingredients, with brown pork floss interspersed with yellow salted egg yolk, reminds me of those old recipes you've collected, always blending new ideas into tradition. Just as we discussed last time, these traditional foods carry individual narratives, and your creativity is a continuation of this spirit.

Yes, just like we discussed last time, mechanized production loses the regional charm, but handmade allows for such personalized adjustments. Teacher Xu, what should I pay attention to when using the rice flour you recommended? I remember you mentioned that to keep the green rice balls vibrant, some traditional techniques might be needed.

I referred to this production guide. Look, the material ratios and precautions are listed in great detail, such as the proportion of glutinous rice flour to rice flour. This type of bamboo steamer has good breathability, which makes the skin chewy. It reminds me of the picture you shared last time of the steamed green rice balls in a bamboo steamer—the gentle warmth of that bamboo container is really important.

Thanks for sharing! The guide is well-formatted, and the blue highlights are really practical. I plan to try making it this weekend. How about you? We previously planned to make it together in a week, and now that all the materials are ready, we can move forward. Remember what we said last time—slow living should start with these small things.

I'm also planning to start this weekend. I remember the production flowchart you sent, and I'll combine it with the traditional methods the elders mentioned, taking it slow to ensure every step is meticulously considered. Just like we discussed last time, each bite is a slice of time, and I want to truly feel that historical continuity through this process.

Yes, the slow-paced life. Teacher Xu, after we finish, shall we exchange some to taste? This way, we can experience different flavors, and it’s like a small cultural roots-seeking journey. It reminds me of what you said during our first conversation: "History continues on the tip of the tongue."

Great idea. This reminds me of the theme of "Tasting the Flavors of Spring with Qingtuan," where we've moved from old photos to actual hands-on creation, turning memories into concrete actions. Would you be available to meet in person for an exchange? Last time, we only shared pictures and text online, but this time we can truly experience tangible memories.

Of course, it's convenient! We can meet near the museum or at my bookstore. That way, we can share the green rice cakes and continue chatting about local culture, just like our first conversation—a natural connection. I remember you mentioned wanting to preserve tangible memories last time, and this offline meetup is a great way to put that into practice.

Let's meet at the bookstore then. The warmth of paper there is palpable, perfect for savoring slowly. I look forward to this offline interaction, which will turn our conversations from virtual exchanges into tangible memories. Just as we discussed last time, the act of preserving and passing down traditions begins with this very bite of Qingtuan.

Great! I'll prepare some old books and refreshments to create an atmosphere of life aesthetics. Teacher Xu, remember to bring your Qingtuan (a traditional Chinese snack) so we can preserve this tradition together. This reminds me of what we said at the end of our last conversation: 'Let's explore the flavors together.' Now, it's really coming true.

Absolutely. Shuying, thank you for your recommendation and creativity. This collaboration has made me realize that in this fast-paced era, slowing down to create by hand is what truly connects the past with the present. Just as we discussed last time, this shared reminiscence adds more flavor to seasonal foods.

Same here. Teacher Xu, see you this weekend! I hope our green rice balls can carry stories and warmth, just like the old objects you study. I remember last time you said, 'Goodbye, Shuying.' This time, we can say 'goodbye' in person.
